title: Labour: Don't Change Course; Help to Turbo-Charge It
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Reacting to England's strong PISA results relative to Wales and Scotland, education writer Tom Sherrington argues that a decade of sustained curriculum, instructional-teaching, and behaviour reform deserves credit — and criticizes the Labour government's Education Secretary for being unable to acknowledge this without lapsing into partisan point-scoring against her Conservative predecessors. He drafts the statement he thinks Powell should have made: crediting a well-defined curriculum, instructional teaching, and secure reading foundations, while also widening technical education and oracy. His central complaint is that some on the left treat curriculum coherence, strong behaviour systems, and instructional teaching as inherently 'right wing,' which he calls an ideological roadblock that misunderstands how learning actually happens in classrooms. He traces this pattern back to David Miliband's 'personalised learning' drive in the 2000s as an earlier instance of Labour education policy being long on rhetoric and short on practicality. Sherrington's overall argument is that England is 'halfway up the mountain' on a hard-won cross-party consensus around curriculum and instruction, and that Labour should build on and extend that progress — adding oracy and rebalancing assessment for lower-attaining students — rather than treating the PISA moment as an opportunity to change direction.
points: Argues England's comparatively strong PISA results versus Wales and Scotland reflect a decade of sustained curriculum, instructional-teaching, and behaviour reform.
Criticizes the Education Secretary for treating acknowledgment of that progress as politically unacceptable because of who gets credit.
Calls it 'nonsense' to frame curriculum coherence, behaviour systems, and instructional teaching as inherently right-wing rather than simply what works in classrooms.
Draws a direct historical parallel to David Miliband's 2000s personalised-learning agenda as '90% wishful rhetoric; 10% practicalities.'
Proposes building on the current consensus with oracy and rebalanced assessment rather than a wholesale change of direction.
quotes: However, the pattern for England seems to be clear enough in relation to Wales and Scotland as to suggest that there’s a strong likelihood that the comparatively strong outcomes are product of what has been a sustained set of agendas over the last decade.
It has the vibe of a non-expert with lay person’s general knowledge preaching to a room of actual experts - which is annoying in any profession.

It’s just absolute nonsense, folly, for people on the left to align those things with a right wing agenda. It just puts a massive ideological roadblock in the way of actually improving education of so many people.
This issue with Labour has a long history, going back to David Miliband’s absurdly undeliverable personalised learning drive in the 2000s. 90% wishful rhetoric; 10% practicalities.

The curriculum has been stable enough, the teaching and learning agenda sustained enough and the discourse around behaviour coherent enough for a consensus to have emerged that is starting to pay dividends.

What should remain is that teachers continue to focus on improving ever more effective and inclusive instructional teaching, creating an excellent curriculum experience across a range of subjects, with strong knowledge foundations, all supported by clear, supportive behaviour routines and cultures.
